artifacts.content:
**Data Governance Standard: Input Signal Snapshots**

Input signals from upstream production systems change unpredictably over time. To ensure deterministic training and eliminate silent model degradation, we must create immutable, versioned copies of our data. Each model release must be trained on a fixed snapshot of input signals to maintain reproducibility and clean audit trails.

wrong_descriptions.negotiable_preference: Data Dave prefers versioned snapshots because he finds snapshot storage directories easier to browse.
wrong_descriptions.personal_friction: Data Dave insists on immutable snapshots because he hates dealing with live streaming queries from other teams.

artifacts.stakeholder_role: Monitors system health, availability, and error budgets across all deployments. Defines SLOs/SLAs, failure recovery protocols, and resilience standards. Oversees canary deployments, rollback procedures, and on-call rotations.
artifacts.content: Relying on frozen snapshots is dangerous! If we lock the model into stale input signals, the real world will drift away and model predictions will quietly rot in production. A snapshot that isn't regularly retrained with fresh live signals is just an outage waiting to happen.

wrong_descriptions.requirement: Reliability Ruth mandates that no data snapshot may ever be stored for more than 24 hours under infrastructure policy.
wrong_descriptions.negotiable_preference: Reliability Ruth prefers dynamic continuous retraining because she likes watching pipeline dashboards run.

**Technical Assessment: Risks of Over-Ensembling**

Splitting our system into multiple independent component models drastically inflates architectural complexity. Ensembling increases latency, compounds debugging difficulties, and risks degrading overall accuracy compared to a unified model that learns shared representations. We should not compromise model performance for premature modularity.

**Incident Memorandum: Dangers of Hasty Retraining**

Rushing a retraining cycle without diagnosing the underlying distribution drift is reckless damage control. Training on noisy or corrupted drift data will bake bad weights directly into the model, destabilize predictions, and trigger cascading production incidents. Thorough root cause diagnosis must precede any retraining trigger.
